tasks.title: Passage 1
tasks.instructions: Read the passage and choose the correct answers. /4 x 2 = 8 points/
tasks.text:
In many European cities, the bicycle has become one of the most popular ways to get to work. In Copenhagen, for example, almost half of all trips to work or school are made by bike. This was not always the case. In the 1970s, the city's streets were full of cars, and cycling was seen as slow and dangerous.

Things began to change when oil prices rose sharply and many people could no longer afford to drive every day. The city government built separate lanes for cyclists and special traffic lights for **them**. Over the following decades, it invested more and more in cycling, and people slowly changed their habits.

Today, cycling is not only cheap but also healthy and good for the environment. Studies show that people who cycle regularly take fewer sick days, and the city has much cleaner air than before. Other cities around the world are now trying to <u>imitate</u> Copenhagen's success.

tasks.title: Listening
tasks.instructions: You are going to listen to a radio presenter interviewing a young café owner. Read each question and choose the correct answer. You have 1 minute and 30 seconds to look through the questions before you listen. You will listen to the passage twice only, so listen carefully. /6 x 2 = 12 points/
tasks.audioScript:
Presenter: Welcome back to 'Young Talents'. My guest today is a nineteen-year-old who has just opened her own café. Welcome!
Guest: Thank you for inviting me.
Presenter: Can you tell our listeners your name?
Guest: Sure. I'm Khulan Batsaikhan. Khulan is spelt K-H-U-L-A-N.
Presenter: Khulan, when did you first become interested in cooking?
Guest: When I was about eleven. My grandmother ran a small restaurant, and I helped her every weekend.
Presenter: And now you have your own café. That's amazing at nineteen!
Guest: Well, I didn't do it alone. My older brother manages the money, and two friends from college work with me.
Presenter: What's special about your café?
Guest: We use only local ingredients: milk, meat and berries from Mongolian farms. And every dish on the menu is under ten thousand tugriks, because I want students to be able to eat there.
Presenter: Is it busy?
Guest: Very! At lunchtime there's usually a queue outside. In the evenings it's quieter, so I'm thinking of starting cooking classes then.
Presenter: Great idea. What do you do to relax?
Guest: Honestly, I don't have much free time, but I go hiking with my dog on Sundays, and I love reading cookbooks, which is still work, I suppose!
Presenter: Khulan, thank you so much.
